1324.title: The Ravidassia community
1324.hook: a community who revere Guru Ravidas and now keep their own scripture
1324.howItsDone: The Ravidassia community revere Guru Ravidas as their Guru and keep a scripture of his hymns in their places of worship; Sikhs continue to sing Ravidas's hymns as part of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, beyond caste names: Singh and Kaur, one shared name so nobody could read your birth off it. Your line was one name for all.

A hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib carries the name Ravidas, the poet tradition remembers as a shoemaker of Benares. In a gurdwara, it's sung as one voice among many in a great book. Across town, under a different symbol, the same words are sung as the voice of the one the room calls Guru. Same poet, same words, a different center. Year three met the community who keep Ravidas at that center. Since then, something has changed in how they keep him.
screen: `ONE VOICE AMONG MANY.` → `THE SAME WORDS, ANOTHER ROOM.` → `A DIFFERENT CENTER.`

segments.voice: First, who they are. The Ravidassia community revere Guru Ravidas as their Guru. It includes families from the same communities Ravidas came from, the ones the old order counted low. For them, a shoemaker who sang his way past every wall of caste is not one voice among many. He is the voice. Second, what has changed. For a long time, the Guru Granth Sahib was installed in Ravidassia places of worship, just as in a gurdwara. In recent years, the community has gathered Guru Ravidas's own hymns into a scripture of their own, and now install it at the center of their worship, with their own greeting and their own symbol too. Third, a hymn to hold it all. In the Granth, in Raag Sorath, Ravidas sings a chain of pictures to God, in paraphrase: you are the sandalwood, I am the water. You are the cloud, I am the peacock. You are the lamp, I am the wick. You are the master, I am the servant. In each pair, the lesser thing is never thrown away. Water takes the scent of sandalwood. The wick is what lets the lamp burn. A low thing, held close to God, becomes part of the light. Fourth, how to stand toward this. Sikhs keep singing Ravidas in the Granth with full honor. The Ravidassia community keep him at the center of a path that is now their own. Some on both sides feel the parting deeply; others call it a community finding its own name. Neither story needs ranking. The same hymns are still sung in both houses.
screen: `RAVIDAS AT THE CENTER.` · `A SCRIPTURE OF THEIR OWN.` · `THE LAMP AND THE WICK.` · `SUNG IN BOTH HOUSES.` · then, large: `THEIR OWN PATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a group that once shared a home with yours, a congregation, a club, a circle of friends, and then went its own way, and let anything that still stings be there. Then picture them at their own table, singing their own song, and wish them well there. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru.
The Ravidassia community. Those who revere Guru Ravidas as their Guru and now keep a scripture of his hymns at the center of their worship. Today's word.
Your line: their own path. Respect starts with the name people give themselves. Same time tomorrow.

1325.title: The Harmandir's day
1325.hook: the Granth is carried in a palki to rest at night and returned at dawn
1325.howItsDone: At the Harmandir Sahib the Guru Granth Sahib is brought out in a palki before dawn for the prakash and carried back at night for sukhasan; gurdwaras and homes that keep the Granth follow the same pattern on a smaller scale.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ravidassia community, keeping Guru Ravidas at the center of a path now their own. Your line was their own path.

Amritsar, before first light. The water around the Harmandir Sahib is black and flat, and the gold looks almost gray. People wait along the causeway, some barefoot on cold marble, some with children asleep on their shoulders. Then a drum, and a conch, and the crowd begins to move. Hands reach out to touch the poles of something being carried. A palki, a palanquin, is coming home. Inside it is a book, wrapped in cloth, and the people reaching for it call that book the Guru. This path has watched the night crossing once already. Today, the whole day around it.
screen: `AMRITSAR, BEFORE DAWN.` → `A DRUM, A CONCH, A CROWD.` → `A PALKI COMES HOME.`

segments.voice: Begin before the light. In the Japji, Guru Nanak points to the ambrosial hours, the early dark before dawn, in paraphrase: in those hours, dwell on the true Name and its greatness. The Harmandir's day starts there. The Granth is carried from its night room, set on its high seat under a canopy, and opened. Sikhs call this the prakash, the light. A hymn is read from the opened page: the Guru's word for that morning. Then the long middle. All day, singers take turns in the sanctum, set after set, while people cross the causeway, bow, listen for a moment, and move on. The doors stay open. The kitchen keeps feeding. The Guru is, in Sikh language, holding court. Then night. After the evening prayers, the Granth is closed, wrapped, and carried out in the palki to rest. Sikhs call this sukhasan, the seat of ease. Not storage. Rest. So why carry a book to bed? Because Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib not as a book they own but as the living Guru, the one Guru Gobind Singh named before he died. A living Guru wakes, gives the word, keeps company, and rests. The ritual is about how you'd treat someone you revere if they lived in your house. Gurdwaras do a version of this in a quiet back room, and so do homes that keep the Granth. At the Harmandir it happens in front of the crowd.
screen: `THE AMBROSIAL HOURS BEFORE DAWN.` · `PRAKASH: THE GURU OPENED FOR THE DAY.` · `ALL DAY, THE HYMNS SUNG ON.` · `SUKHASAN: CARRIED TO REST.` · then, large: `A LIVING GURU WAKES AND RESTS.`

segments.voice: See the causeway in the dark, the palki on the shoulders of the crowd, the drum and the conch; then the evening, the same palki going the other way, and between the two crossings a whole day of hymns. Breathe in at the dawn crossing and out at the night one, resting on Waheguru if you pray.
The Harmandir's day. The Granth opened at dawn in the prakash, sung all day, and carried at night in the palki to rest, in sukhasan. Today's word.
Your line: carried to rest. Live video from the Harmandir is streamed online, palki and all. Rest well tonight.

1326.title: The Akal Takht today
1326.hook: the rebuilt Takht faces the Harmandir across the causeway
1326.howItsDone: Pilgrims at Amritsar visit both the Harmandir Sahib and the Akal Takht, which face each other across the courtyard; the Guru Granth Sahib rests at the Akal Takht complex at night and returns to the Harmandir at dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Harmandir's day: prakash at dawn, hymns all day, and the Granth carried to rest at night. Your line was carried to rest.

Stand on the marble at the edge of the pool in Amritsar and turn slowly. In front of you, out on the water at the end of the causeway, the Harmandir Sahib, low and gold, full of singing. Behind you, on dry land, a tall white building with a gold dome. You can't look at both at once. You have to turn. Last night's palki crossed between them. Today, the second building as it stands now, and the line that runs between the two.
screen: `TURN SLOWLY ON THE MARBLE.` → `ONE ON THE WATER, ONE ON LAND.` → `YOU HAVE TO TURN.`

segments.voice: First, the building. The Akal Takht you see today has been rebuilt. This path told that story on an earlier day: after it was wrecked, Sikhs insisted on raising it again by their own hands, as kar seva. So it's new stone on old ground, and the place, Sikhs say, is what carries the authority. Second, the line. Tradition says Guru Hargobind raised his seat facing the Harmandir. Walk the causeway back, through the gateway at its end, and the Takht stands just beyond. One stands in the water, the other is raised on land. Third, what each one does. In the Harmandir, the Guru's hymns are sung from before dawn into the night. From the Akal Takht, the panth's decisions are made and its letters go out, as you heard on an earlier day. One is for listening, one is for answering, and neither has its back to the other. Fourth, the name over the second door. The opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib describe God as akaal moorat, in paraphrase: a form beyond time. Akal, the Timeless. So the building that deals with worldly things, quarrels and rulings and the panth's business, carries the name of what is beyond time. Every night the Granth makes the crossing between them, the word carried across to where the decisions are made.
screen: `NEW STONE ON OLD GROUND.` · `ONE ON THE WATER, ONE RAISED ON LAND.` · `ONE FOR LISTENING, ONE FOR ANSWERING.` · `AKAL: THE TIMELESS.` · then, large: `FACING EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: See the Harmandir in front of you, low and gold on the water, and breathe in, listening for the singing. Turn slowly to the Akal Takht behind you, raised and white, and breathe out with one decision that's waiting for you this week. Turn back and forth a few times, and let the two face each other inside you.
The Akal Takht today. The rebuilt throne of the Timeless at Amritsar, raised on land and facing the Harmandir across the courtyard. Today's word.
Your line: facing each other. Listening and answering, side by side, across one courtyard. Until tomorrow.

1327.title: Bangla Sahib
1327.hook: in Delhi, the gurdwara of the child Guru, with its healing pool
1327.howItsDone: Visitors to Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, eat in the langar, and sit by the sarovar; some take its water home for family members who are unwell.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akal Takht, new stone on old ground, facing the Harmandir across the courtyard. Your line was facing each other.

A plastic bottle, the kind you'd buy at any corner shop, sits on a kitchen shelf in a Delhi apartment. Nobody drinks from it casually. It was filled at the edge of a pool in the middle of the city, carried home on the metro, and kept for when someone in the house is unwell. A grandmother pours a little into a steel cup and hands it over without a word. The pool is at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, near one of the city's big traffic circles. Year one told how the child Guru came to Delhi. Today, the place he left behind, and the water.
screen: `A BOTTLE ON A KITCHEN SHELF.` → `KEPT FOR WHEN SOMEONE IS UNWELL.` → `FILLED AT A POOL IN DELHI.`

segments.voice: First, the house. Bangla means bungalow. Tradition says Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru and still a child, stayed here in the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh when he was called to Delhi. While he was there, an epidemic swept the city, and the child went out among the sick of every faith. He caught the disease himself and died in Delhi. The bungalow became a gurdwara. Second, the water. Tradition says the house's well gave the water the young Guru blessed and handed to the sick. Today a wide pool, a sarovar, lies beside the gurdwara, and people sit by it, touch the water to their eyes, and fill bottles to take home. Some Sikhs add a caution: the water isn't a charm; what it carries is the memory of a child who served. Third, a hymn. In Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan gives thanks, in paraphrase: the Beloved has given protection from smallpox; the Supreme Lord has shown mercy. Tradition links that hymn to Guru Arjan's young son, the boy who would become Guru Hargobind, when he fell ill. So, as tradition reads it, the Granth holds a father's relief over a sick child. At Bangla Sahib the story turns around: here it's the child who goes to the sick. Fourth, Sikhs say the same light passed from Guru to Guru, whatever the body's age. At Bangla Sahib you can see what that light did in a small body: it didn't hide from a sick city.

1328.title: Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj
1328.hook: where Guru Tegh Bahadur was killed and where his body was cremated
1328.howItsDone: Sikhs visiting Delhi go to Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Chandni Chowk and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj, and both are crowded on the day Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom is remembered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bangla Sahib, where the child Guru went out to the sick, and the pool beside it. Your line was the child's gurdwara.

Car horns. A man pushing a cart stacked with sacks. A wedding-card shop, a sweet shop, a rickshaw wedged sideways in the lane. Old Delhi's great market street, Chandni Chowk, is loud from morning to night. And right in the middle of it, between the stalls, a gurdwara with a white front and a gold dome, its singing drifting out into the traffic. Across the city stands a second gurdwara tied to the same day. Two buildings, one death. Today, why it takes two.
screen: `CAR HORNS, CARTS, A SWEET SHOP.` → `A GURDWARA AMONG THE STALLS.` → `TWO BUILDINGS, ONE DEATH.`

segments.voice: First, Sis Ganj. Sis is the Punjabi word for head. Year one told the story: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, would not give up his faith, nor let others be forced from theirs, and he was beheaded in the open square of Chandni Chowk. Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands at that spot, right in the market, and tradition says it keeps the trunk of the tree under which he was killed. Second, Rakab Ganj. This path has met both carriers: Bhai Jaita, who took the head north to Anandpur, and Lakhi Shah Vanjara, who took the body home and set his own house alight. Tradition says Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands where that house burned. Third, why two. Danger split the Guru's body two ways, and the panth would not lose either. It marked the place of the death and the place of the fire, and kept walking to both: one in the loud middle of a market, open to anyone between errands, the other marking a fire lit in secret by a man with a cart. Fourth, a line from the Guru's own saloks near the end of the Granth, in paraphrase: whatever has come into being will pass away, today or tomorrow; so sing the praises of the Lord, and let the other tangles go. He wrote about the body passing. Then his own body passed, and two ordinary men made sure it was honored. Two addresses for one gift.
screen: `SIS GANJ: WHERE HE GAVE HIS HEAD.` · `RAKAB GANJ: WHERE THE HOUSE BURNED.` · `TWO PLACES, NEITHER LOST.` · `WHATEVER COMES INTO BEING PASSES.` · then, large: `TWO ADDRESSES FOR ONE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Hear the horns, the carts, the shopkeepers calling, and let the noise be there. Then walk, in your mind, through the open doors of Sis Ganj and let the noise fall behind you, standing quietly where the market once watched a man refuse to be moved. Step back out into the street carrying a little of that quiet, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru.
Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj. Two gurdwaras in Delhi: one where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded, one where his body was secretly cremated. Today's word.

1329.title: Nankana Sahib
1329.howItsDone: Sikh pilgrims cross into Pakistan to visit Nankana Sahib, especially for Guru Nanak's birth anniversary, and go from gurdwara to gurdwara, each marking a story from his childhood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj, two places in Delhi for one death, and two ordinary men who did the carrying. Your line was where he gave his head.

Some families keep a map of a child's first years without ever drawing one. That's the bench where she learned to ride a bike. That's the corner shop where he spent his first coin. Point at a street and someone says, that's where it happened. Now give that habit to a whole people, about one boy, in one small town in Punjab. The town was called Talwandi. Today it's called Nankana Sahib, and its streets are a family map of a childhood.
screen: `A MAP OF A CHILD'S FIRST YEARS.` → `THAT'S WHERE IT HAPPENED.` → `ONE TOWN, ONE BOY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition says Guru Nanak was born in the village of Talwandi, which later came to be called Nankana Sahib, after him. Today it sits in Pakistan, as this path has told before. Second, the map. Gurdwara Janam Asthan, the birthplace, stands where tradition says the house was. One gurdwara marks where the boy played with other children. Patti Sahib marks the school where, tradition says, he learned his letters and surprised his teacher with what he did with them. One marks the field where the cattle he was minding wandered into a neighbor's crop, and, in the story, the crop was found unharmed. One marks the tree where, in the story, a cobra spread its hood to shade him as he slept. Year one told those stories. Here, they have addresses. Third, how to hold a map like that. These places rest on the janamsakhis, and Sikhs read them in different ways: some as plain history, some as loving pictures of who Nanak was. Either way, the map remembers him not as a figure who appeared fully grown, but as a boy who played, went to school, minded cattle, fell asleep in a field. Fourth, the light. The poet Bhai Gurdas describes the moment Guru Nanak came into the world, in paraphrase: when the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread through the world. Nankana Sahib is the small picture beside that big one: a town where you can stand on the spot and say, it began here.
screen: `TALWANDI BECAME NANKANA SAHIB.` · `A TOWN MAPPED BY A CHILDHOOD.` · `HISTORY, OR LOVING PICTURES.` · `THE MIST CLEARED, AND LIGHT SPREAD.` · then, large: `WHERE IT BEGAN.`

segments.voice: See a small town on the Punjab plain, flat fields, low houses, and a boy running between them: a school with slates, a field with cattle, a tree with deep shade. Let it be ordinary. Then bring to mind the place where your own story began, a house, a street, a town, and rest in both pictures for a few breaths, with Waheguru if you pray.
Nankana Sahib. The town once called Talwandi, where tradition says Guru Nanak was born, with gurdwaras marking the stories of his childhood. Today's word.
Your line: where it began. Every life starts somewhere you could point to. Rest well.

1330.title: Kartarpur Sahib
1330.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit Gurdwara Kartarpur Sahib, across the border in Pakistan, through the Kartarpur corridor; Sikhs remember it as the place where Guru Nanak farmed, built a community and died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nankana Sahib, a town mapped by a childhood. Your line was where it began.

A pair of hands, cracked at the knuckles, soil under the nails. A tea glass on a wall at the edge of a field. Somewhere a tractor coughs and goes quiet. In flat farmland near the river Ravi, a white gurdwara rises out of the green, and the fields come almost up to its walls. Yesterday, where Guru Nanak's life began. Today, where it ended, and what he did with the years between: he went home to the soil.
screen: `SOIL UNDER THE NAILS.` → `A WHITE GURDWARA IN THE FIELDS.` → `HOME TO THE SOIL.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Kartarpur, the Creator's town, as year one told. Tradition says Guru Nanak settled here after his long journeys, farmed his own land, gathered a community around hymns, work and a shared kitchen, and died here. Today the gurdwara stands among fields on the Pakistani side of the border, and pilgrims come through the corridor this path met on an earlier day. Second, the hymn. In Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak turns a farmer's work into a picture of the inner life, in paraphrase: make your mind the farmer, good deeds the work, effort the water, and your body the field. Sow the Name as the seed. Let contentment be the plank that levels the soil, and humility the fence around it. It's practical: a farmer can't skip the water or forget the fence, and neither, in the hymn, can a seeker. Third, why it matters that he farmed. After all those roads, the great teacher could have lived on gifts. Tradition says he chose a plow. So when Sikhs speak of earning by honest work, they can point to a field and say, that's where he farmed. Fourth, the end of the story, told briefly because year one told it fully. Tradition says that when he died here, Hindus and Muslims who both loved him laid flowers on either side of him. Today a memorial and a grave stand side by side at Kartarpur. A field, a hymn about a field, and a farmer people of two faiths wouldn't let go.
screen: `THE CREATOR'S TOWN, AMONG FIELDS.` · `MIND THE FARMER, BODY THE FIELD.` · `HE CHOSE A PLOW.` · `A MEMORIAL AND A GRAVE, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `WHERE HE FARMED.`

segments.voice: See flat green land running to the edge of sight, a white gurdwara in the middle, and a man in plain clothes walking a furrow early, before the heat. Then walk your own field for a minute, the mind as the farmer and the body as the field, and just notice what seed you're sowing today and what fence keeps it safe. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru.
Kartarpur Sahib. The Creator's town, where tradition says Guru Nanak farmed his own land, gathered a community, and died. Today's word.
Your line: where he farmed. Contentment levels the soil, and humility is the fence. See you tomorrow.
